Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock finished down 8.1% on Tuesday, Nov. 24, as investors retreated from the same chip stocks they couldn't get enough of a day earlier.

The Nasdaq Composite sank 1.5%, while the S&P 500 fell 0.5%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Chip stocks' Nvidia-fueled rally reversed on Tuesday

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA)'s decision to bring back CEO Jensen Huang set off a huge rally across chip stocks on Monday as investors reacted to the stunning reversal just a week after the board told investors it wasn't an option. The Nasdaq had its best day since April of 2025.

But that rally reversed sharply today as investors digested what his return will mean in the long term and how it will affect chip rivals -- like Intel.

Intel's new foundry customer has an unclear payoff

Just last week, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the company had landed its first outside customer for 18A-P, an advanced manufacturing process important to the company's turnaround efforts. It's a positive step, but details were light, so it's unclear how much financial impact it will actually have.

Intel's foundry business posted a $1.85 billion operating loss last quarter, with the company's finance chief indicating the company probably won't generate positive free cash flow -- the cash left over after paying for investments like new factories -- next year as it keeps investing in manufacturing.

Image source: Getty Images.

Long term, I think that will pay off. I'm just not jumping in any time soon given the current market.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) plunged 8.86% on Tuesday, November 24, closing at $413.27 as renewed selling pressure swept across the semiconductor industry.

Trading volume reached 45.7 million shares, approximately 64% above its three-month daily average of 27.8 million, reflecting heightened investor activity amid the latest sell-off.

How the markets moved today

S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 0.50% to 7,201, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) declined 1.48% to 23,734. Among semiconductor peers, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) closed at $155.38, down 5.86%, and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) closed at $54.80, down 8.15%, underscoring the pressure across the chipmakers.

What this means for investors

AMD's latest sell-off highlights growing uncertainty surrounding the financial implications of large-scale AI partnerships. Adding to these concerns, the company recently filed a registration covering approximately 337 million shares for potential resale, raising questions about future shareholder dilution. Although the filing does not represent an immediate sale of shares, investors should consider how these arrangements could affect existing shareholders and prices.

Despite the recent volatility, AMD's underlying business continues to demonstrate strong growth. The company recently reported record quarterly revenue and raised its outlook, supported by demand for its data center processors and AI accelerators.

Looking ahead, AMD's ability to translate growing AI demand into sustained profitability will be critical. While the recent decline could present an attractive entry point, the combination of potential dilution, competitive pressures, and elevated semiconductor valuations warrants caution.

title: Applied Materials vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Applied Materials vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 2:50 PM EST 6 min read
AMAT
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

As chip demand evolves, investors must decide between Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC). Both play vital roles in the global tech ecosystem but currently travel very different financial paths.

Applied Materials provides the essential machinery used to fabricate advanced electronics, while Intel designs and manufactures the chips that power computers and data centers. Comparing them highlights the choice between a steady equipment leader and a legacy manufacturer in the midst of a massive structural turnaround.

The case for Applied Materials

Applied Materials provides specialized equipment and software for the fabrication of semiconductors and advanced displays. It serves a global customer base including logic, DRAM, and NAND memory manufacturers. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as two specific customers accounted for roughly 19% and 15% of net revenue in the latest annual report.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 25, 2026, revenue reached about $34.4 billion, representing growth of approximately 21.4% compared to the prior year. Net income for this period was about $10.1 billion, a significant increase from the roughly $7.0 billion reported in the previous year. This growth highlights the ongoing demand for sophisticated production tools among semiconductor stocks.

As of its October 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x. This ratio compares total debt to the value of shareholder equity, measuring how much a company relies on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a firm's ability to pay off its short-term obligations using assets it can convert to cash within a year, is roughly 2.3x. In the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, 2026, free cash flow was approximately $6.2 billion.

The case for Intel

Intel designs and manufactures processors and accelerators for cloud, enterprise, and PC markets. The company is currently pursuing an IDM 2.0 strategy, which involves expanding its own manufacturing capacity to serve external third-party customers through its foundry segment. Its three largest customers are highly concentrated, accounting for approximately 43% of net revenue in its latest annual report.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached about $59.9 billion, a growth of roughly 12.1% over the prior twelve-month period. Despite the rise in sales, the company reported a net loss of around $12.0 billion. This loss reflects the immense costs associated with Intel's efforts to modernize its fabrication facilities and regain a competitive edge in processor architecture.

Trump Warns of "Paying 200 Percent on Chips" in Two Years. That Pushes TSMC Toward a $22.6 Billion Texas Plant ©@Aaron Hawkins from Getty Images via Canva, @genkur from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

President Trump said foreign chips will face 200% tariffs in two years, and a filing shows TSMC weighing a $22.6 billion Texas plant.

TSMC can afford US fabs, but management expects overseas fabs to cut its gross margin by 3% to 4% in the next few years.

Analysts haven't left room for that, and TSMC's mid-January guidance is the next test.

Nvidia looks better placed than Apple to pay more for US-made chips, and Intel gets a rival on its home turf.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM:NYSE) jumped 10% in Taipei on Tuesday after Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) brought back Jensen Huang as CEO.

But the day before, on CNBC's Squawk on the Street, President Donald Trump said something that matters more for TSMC and customers like Apple (AAPL:NASDAQ). Talking about Taiwan's hold on the chip business, he gave a timeline:

"in two years they're going to be paying 200 percent on chips."

He credited TSMC CEO C.C. Wei and said Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) once had a leader who wanted chip tariffs, "but no president had the guts to do it."

Then came the most telling line: "By the way, if I announce that there's no tariffs anymore, they would stop building immediately and they would love it."

That's about as honest as industrial policy gets. A US fab is the toll for selling chips into America.

Texas is the next toll booth

A filing with Texas state officials shows TSMC seeking a property tax limitation for a proposed $22.6 billion chipmaking complex in Brazos County. TSMC hasn't committed yet, and it called the tax break crucial to its decision.

Since Jan. 15, a 25% Section 232 duty has applied to certain advanced chips, and January's US-Taiwan trade deal lets companies with US production import more chips free of that duty.

That's awkward for Intel. Its third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.5 billion, but every TSMC fab in Arizona, and maybe Texas, lets TSMC's customers buy US-made chips without switching foundries.
